newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb jury sees mangled vehicle parts.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb jury sees mangled vehicle parts.

text.p: Jurors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Wednesday were shown pieces of twisted metal and mangled components believed to have come from the rented truck the government says was used in the bombing.

A string of federal agents told how an army of 250 investigators painstakingly combed the area around the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in the days after the April 19, 1995, bombing that killed 168 people.
"We went block to block, alley to alley, sidewalk to sidewalk," FBI supervisor Patrick Daly said, describing the evidence-gathering effort.
Agents scoured an area more than a mile (km) wide, including parking lots, streets and rooftops as well as the federal building itself, collecting more than seven tons of debris, investigators said.

The recovered parts shown to the jury included a steering assembly found embedded in a van in a nearby parking lot. Also displayed was a front axle, two parts of a Ford vehicle logo, a truck rail frame, a wheel rim, a tie rod and other damaged and twisted pieces of metal.
Prosecutors did not immediately explain the significance of the parts but they were believed to belong to the rented Ryder truck that prosecutors say defendant Timothy McVeigh used in the bombing.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch allowed jurors to stand up several times to get a better look at the vehicle parts.
Another FBI agent testified about pieces of melted and burned white plastic that he had found near the bomb site, but what they were was not immediately clear.

Under cross-examination by defence attorney Robert Nigh, Daly conceded that he told FBI agents in his search team to look for things associated with a truck bomb because the government had concluded early on that a truck bomb caused the explosion.
Sources close to the trial said the prosecution could rest its case as early as the beginning of next week, far sooner than had been expected. The defence then presents its case.
McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran with strong anti-government views, has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

Jurors watched attentively as prosecutors showed pictures taken by a video surveillance camera mounted at the Regency Tower apartment building in downtown Oklahoma City in the crucial moments before the bombing.

The grainy black and white pictures clearly showed a Ryder rental truck pull up across the street from the apartment complex and leave seconds later. The truck was similar to the one the prosecution said was used in the blast, but the truck's driver could not be seen in the pictures.
The time stamp automatically indicated on the video tape by the security system showed it leaving a few minutes before the bomb rocked downtown Oklahoma City.

In emotional testimony, a maintenance worker described how, minutes later, the bomb exploded and an axle flew through the air and landed on his car, which was parked a block from the federal building. "I turned and saw a humongous object coming towards us, spinning like a boomerang," Richard Nichols said.
The government says the axle that crushed Nichols' car, narrowly missing his wife and nephew, was the axle from the Ryder truck that has already been introduced into evidence.

Nichols was due to meet his wife and nephew outside the apartment complex at 9 a.m. on the day of the blast to go to a doctor's appointment. Fortunately for Nichols, he was slightly late. Otherwise, he said, his voice breaking with emotion, he would probably have been driving past the Murrah building when the bomb went off.
Prosecutors for the first time on Wednesday focused on the murder counts against McVeigh, who has been accused of murdering eight federal officials.

Former Secret Service agent Lawrence Kingry testified that four slain agents were in the agency's offices in the Murrah building when he left at 8:45 a.m. on the day of the bombing to attend a hearing at the nearby federal courthouse.

When he returned soon after the explosion, he said the offices where Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alan Whicher and special agents Mickey Maroney, Cynthia Campbell-Brown and Donald Leonard had been were gone. "I looked to where our field office would have been and there was nothing there."
The four were later found dead. Kingry, who now works at the Oklahoma state police academy, testified that the agents were killed while performing their official duties.

Regina Bonny, a police narcotics agent assigned to the DEA office in the Murrah building, cried on the witness stand when prosecutors showed pictures of people she knew who died in the blast. One victim, Carrie Lenz, was pregnant and had been showing other office workers ultrasound pictures of the baby she was carrying minutes before the bomb exploded, Bonny said.
